project.title: Plant growth & statistics
project.alt: All thirty PlantGrowth observations shown by control and two treatment groups
project.desc: Explore thirty plant-growth observations, compare the groups and explain what the statistics can—and cannot—support.
project.built: Added a reproducible, visual PlantGrowth investigation alongside the original statistical coursework, preserving all raw observations and explaining uncertainty.
project.why: Differences in averages can be misleading without considering variability. This project shows how visual evidence and statistical testing support a careful comparison.
how: Inspect every observation under control and two treatment conditions, with ten examples per group.
Compare sample means and uncertainty; use Welch ANOVA as the primary omnibus comparison, with classic ANOVA shown as sensitivity analysis.
Examine three pairwise differences using Welch tests and a Bonferroni family adjustment, then interpret the small-sample limits.
project.demonstrates: Statistical reasoning, hypothesis testing, visual communication and explaining uncertainty around a decision.
project.caption: Ten source observations per group, with median/quartile boxes. Every point comes from the preserved PlantGrowth teaching dataset; visual jitter does not alter the measurements.
project.result: Thirty source observations, ten per group. Mean dried weights: control 5.032, treatment 1 4.661, treatment 2 5.526 (dataset units). Welch omnibus p=0.0174; classic equal-variance ANOVA p=0.0159 is shown as a sensitivity analysis. Pairwise comparisons use a three-comparison Bonferroni adjustment. Methods, assumptions and all observations are visible; this small teaching dataset does not establish general treatment effectiveness.
project.limits: Thirty observations in a teaching dataset do not establish universal treatment effectiveness. Independence and the original experimental design cannot be verified from the CSV alone. Mean intervals assume approximate normality; Welch inference is a small-sample approximation. A p-value is neither an effect size nor the probability that the null hypothesis is true. Methods were selected for this educational investigation, not preregistered confirmatory analysis.
project.technical: Source validation checks three groups of ten finite measurements. The reproducible script records dataset SHA-256 and dependency versions, computes Welch and classic one-way ANOVA, pointwise t intervals and three Bonferroni-adjusted Welch pair comparisons. Tests independently reconcile classic F with sums of squares, verify group summaries/multiplicity and reproduce numeric outputs byte-for-byte. Original notebook exercises remain intact.
project.run: Install requirements.txt, run python analyze_plants.py and python -m unittest discover -p "test_*.py" -v. Results, raw source CSV and the original project.ipynb are available in the repository.
